https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/arti.text: Return to Homepage Top Stories: GOP midterm convention Apple iPhone Duo review Amazon cargo plane crash Clancy's ex-husband threatens legal action Brent oil crosses $100 9/11 documents on Ground Zero air quality Meta stock surges Social Security's 2027 COLA U.S.-Canada trade war Miami cargo plane crash CIA Director John Ratcliffe attends a US House Intelligence Committee hearing on worldwide threats, on Capitol Hill in Washington, DC, in March. - Kylie Cooper/Reuters President Donald Trump's central intelligence chief traveled to Moscow this week with a warning to Russia not to stage an attack in NATO territory, among other issues, according to two people familiar with the matter. CIA Director John Ratcliffe also used the trip, which wasn't announced publicly, to encourage Russia to cut off economic and military support for Iran as the administration works to choke off Tehran financially. US intelligence officials in the lead up to the trip assessed that Russia was in an increasingly weak position in its war with Ukraine that could prompt it to take military action against NATO, four sources familiar with the latest intelligence told CNN. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement For Russia, the goal would be to raise the stakes of supporting Ukraine in the grinding conflict and prompt a negotiated settlement favorable to Russia — an "escalate to de-escalate" strategy. Ratcliffe's trip this week was the first known visit by a senior Trump administration official to Moscow in months. The last visit by a CIA director to the Russian capital came under the Biden administration in 2021, when William Burns warned Putin against a full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Russia invaded three months later. CNN has reached out to the CIA. The Wall Street Journal first reported on Ratcliffe's warning in Russia. Although there was no specific intelligence suggesting that Russia was imminently planning on launching an attack, the sources said, a string of intelligence warnings for weeks has indicated that Moscow might take a number of actions, including increased sabotage efforts, cyber or drone attacks, or even a more severe action like a land grab in Europe. Advertisement Advertisement At least one recent intelligence report circulated in the run-up to Ratcliffe's trip assessed that Russian President Vladimir Putin likely believes the US won't risk becoming involved in another conflict because it would run against American public opinion, according to one of the sources. That could give him the confidence to take action, as the consequences of the conflict continue to mount for Russia. Another one of the sources noted that Russia is bogged down on the frontlines in Ukraine, increasingly suffering economically both from western sanctions and from Ukrainian attacks on its energy infrastructure. "They are on their heels," that source said. Trump on Thursday downplayed the prospects of Russia attacking NATO territory and declined to say whether Ratcliffe had issued a warning to Putin. Advertisement Advertisement Trump said his conversations with the Russian president had assured him such a plan was not in the works. "I've had good talks with him. He's not going to be attacking a NATO territory," Trump told CNN's Kristen Holmes in the Oval Office. "I don't want to comment on that, but they're not going to attack," Trump later said when asked about Ratcliffe warning Putin. Earlier this week, Trump denied that was the intent of Ratcliffe's trip. "He's there, you know, very sort of semi-routine," Trump told Glenn Beck in a radio interview on Wednesday. "I hate to disappoint people. We would like to see the war with Ukraine end." Advertisement Advertisement US and western intelligence assessments have indicated Putin could try to test NATO's resolve by launching a limited attack on an allied country within the next few years, CNN has previously reported . How and when Putin might do so remains an open question. But sources have said he is most likely to escalate in some way by targeting the Baltic states — Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania — or Poland. There have been numerous instances over the last few years of Russia encroaching on NATO territory. In May, a drone carrying explosives hit an apartment building in Romania as Russian forces attacked a nearby Ukrainian port, injuring two people. And last September, NATO fighter jets shot down multiple Russian drones that had violated Polish airspace during an attack on Ukraine. And earlier this month, the US assessed that an explosive-laden drone discovered at an airport in Germany belonged to a Russian intelligence service. Advertisement Advertisement Trump has maintained a contentious relationship with NATO, and has lashed out at the alliance's members for not being more supportive of his war against Iran. He has never entirely ruled out attempting to withdraw the US from the bloc. Still, a NATO summit in Turkey last month ended amicably. And he maintains friendly ties with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte. Asked whether Ratcliffe was visiting Moscow to raise concerns about Russian designs on NATO territory or to ask for Russia's help in reopening the Strait of Hormuz, Trump told Beck, "John Ratcliffe is a fantastic guy. He's the head of the CIA, and he is not in there for any of the things that you said." Ratcliffe flew to Moscow aboard a C-17 Globemaster III, a military transport aircraft. According to flight tracking website Flightradar24, the flight initially took off from Joint Base Andrews in Maryland and transited through Riga, the Latvian capital. Advertisement Advertisement Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said the CIA director did not meet with Putin during the trip. He said Ratcliffe's contact with Russia was "more or less at the level of the special services." Peskov added that while this was "positive," it was premature to speculate "whether this will have an effect overall on the process of pulling our bilateral relations out of the deepest crisis they are currently in." The US had asked Ukraine to halt drone and missile strikes in Moscow and other cities in the north of Russia ahead of Ratcliffe's trip, a person familiar with the matter said. The Ukrainians were told a senior US official would be traveling in Russia. This story has been updated with additional developments. CNN's Haley Britzky and Jennifer Hansler contributed to this report. https://www.euronews.com/2026/11/20/trum.text: US President Donald Trump defended his relationships with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin following his four-day trip to Asia, while addressing the wars in Ukraine and Iran and outlining new trade proposals.Trump praised his meetings with both leaders, calling their relationship a "positive" development.He also called critics of his relationships with Putin and Xi "stupid", following criticism of his decision to describe Putin as a "friend".Asked whether Putin was a friend of the United States, Trump said he could not speak for the country, but described his relationship with the Russian leader as "fantastic" and a "very good thing"."He's got lots of nuclear — he's second to us in nuclear weapons, it's very good. I think it, I think it gives us a lot of additional strength. And he's having a hard time right now because he's in a war that should have lasted one day and it's lasted for five years".Russia-Ukraine war: Trump says Putin wants to end the conflictTurning to the war in Ukraine, Trump said Putin had expressed a desire to end the conflict "by diplomatic means".However, Trump acknowledged difficulties in reaching a peace agreement, blaming tensions between Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy."The problem is President Zelenskyy and President Putin have tremendous hatred, and that's never easy," he told reporters, adding: "We're trying to help them [...]. They don't know how to end it. They want to end it. They're both stuck in it".Asked about security guarantees for Ukraine: “We don’t want to talk about security guarantees yet, because first we need the deal.”While the war is still ongoing, US, Russian and Chinese leaders issued a joint peace declaration in China, pledging to "maintain strategic stability and international security". They also outlined shared ambitions to reform the UN and keep the International Criminal Court in check.Trump says he wants a ‘real deal’ with IranOn the ongoing conflict with Iran, Trump said Tehran wanted an agreement with Washington but had yet to offer acceptable terms."We want to make a real deal, not a fake deal," he said, accusing the Iranian government of "bull-----ing people for 51 years."Trump also predicted further falls in US petrol prices, although he acknowledged that much would depend on how the conflict with Iran is resolved. Despite his claim that petrol prices have fallen recently, they remain around €0.13 per litre higher nationwide than when he took office.The President also warned that Washington would not allow Iran to develop a so-called dirty bomb, citing unconfirmed reports."There is a rumor that they're building a dirty bomb," he told reporters. "We will not allow that."Trade deals with Mexico and CanadaTrump said the US was "getting close to a deal" with Mexico following talks with President Claudia Sheinbaum, but insisted that Washington would not accept a trade surplus in Mexico's favour."We can't have you have a surplus," Trump said he told Sheinbaum. "We're not going to let that happen."On Canada, Trump said "more work remains to be done", accusing the country of taking advantage of the US in trade for years.He also said Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney wanted to revive the Keystone pipeline project, but warned that Canada would need to offer further concessions before an agreement could be reached.Heavy taxes on US data centres built abroadTrump also announced plans to impose heavy taxes on American companies building data centres overseas, saying he wanted the facilities to remain in the United States."We're not allowing data centres to go into other countries," he told reporters, warning that companies could face "a tremendous tax".The President offered no further details and acknowledged that he had not yet discussed the proposal with his own officials.He also encouraged Americans to support data centre projects in their communities while negotiating benefits from developers.

A joint initiative of the U.S. Department of State and the U.S. Department of Education, International Education Week is an effort to promote programs that prepare Americans for a global environment and to attract future leaders from abroad to study in the United States. This year’s theme is “Bridging Cultures, Bridging Borders.” “Through our International Education Week activities, we hope to build global awareness and appreciation between the different cultures represented here at TROY,” said Maria Frigge, Dean of International Student Services. “We hope all departments, faculty, staff and students will engage in the many different activities we have scheduled throughout the week.” People are also reading… City of Auburn addresses criticism surrounding mosque Auburn football quarterback Byrum Brown still questionable for Iron Bowl Injury report: Alex Golesh gives update on trio of Auburn players ahead of Iron Bowl Restaurants offering Thanksgiving meals in Auburn and Opelika Auburn teens arrested on swatting charges, Auburn police say Facility closures and garbage routes in Auburn and Opelika over Thanksgiving holiday HIGH SCHOOL FOOTBALL SCOREBOARD: Auburn High, Loachapoka, Central-Phenix City and Reeltown to the semifinals Longtime Auburn basketball student manager Sam Cunningham is cured of cancer How did Alex Golesh assess performance of backup quarterback Tristan Ti’a? 6 local high school football prospects Auburn University needs to recruit Auburn vs. Samford: Our reporters make their picks Report Card: Auburn football vs. Samford East Alabama Medical Center moves to "B" grade in national hospital safety rating 4 takeaways after Auburn football demolishes Samford on senior day Four takeaways, two touchdowns: Auburn High’s defense shows out in Hewitt-Trussville rematch Activities will take place throughout the week on the Troy Campus, culminating with the annual ISCO Festival, hosted by TROY’s International Student Cultural Organization, at 5:30 p.m. on Nov. 19 in the Lamar P. Higgins Ballrooms, located on the second floor of the Trojan Center. Tickets are $10 for students and $15 for non-students. Tickets will go on sale Nov. 12 and can be purchased in the International Student Services office, 007 Hawkins Hall from 8 a.m. to noon or 1 to 5 p.m. or at the ISCO table in the Trojan Center Food Court each day from 11 a.m. to 1 p.m. International Education Week schedule Sunday, Nov. 15 Soccer tournament, 11 a.m., Intramural Fields Monday, Nov. 16 3:30 p.m., Trojan Center 119, Destination Desserts – Real Students. Real Stories. Come and try international desserts and hear from Troy University students that have studied at partner schools abroad. Hear from students that are currently studying at Troy University that are from the University’s international partner schools. 6 p.m., Academic Quad, TROY to the World Christmas Tree Lighting Ceremony 6:30 p.m., Baptist Campus Ministries, Table Tennis Tournament 6:30 p.m., Wright Hall Gym, Badminton Tournament Tuesday, Nov. 17 11:30 a.m. to 1 p.m., Trojan Center Food Court, Beyond Borders: The Global Trivia Challenge Wednesday, Nov. 18 11 a.m. to 1 p.m., Academic Quad, Taste of the World, featuring a Global Bake Off, a Study Abroad Station, World Languages Corner, Henna Art, Dress the Part, K-Edu Center activities and games, and Snapshots of the World photo displays 4 p.m., Troy Campus Library, America in the World at 250 Roundtable Discussion. Over 250 years of its existence, the United States has been a powerful influence in the world. The roundtable of Troy University history and political science professors – Dr. Tim Buckner, Dr. Joel Campbell, Dr. David Carlson, Dr. Margaret K. Gnoinska, and Dr. Dan Puckett – will discuss patterns, tensions, and contradictions in America’s foreign relations. They will focus on the early republic, the Civil War, the interwar period and WWII, the Cold War, and the post-Cold War period, taking us to the present-day U.S. foreign policy and its impact on the world. The event is organized by the Department of History and Philosophy, sponsored by the College of Arts and Humanities, and made available by the Troy University Library. The event is open to the public. Light refreshments will be provided. Thursday, Nov. 20 12 to 1:30 p.m., Upstairs Dining Hall, Taste + Create: Korean Gimbap. Want to learn how to make Korean Gimbap? Join the International Office and the Jeonnam Glocal K-EDU Center for the Taste + Create event! All materials will be provided, so just grab a few friends and join us for a fun lunch where you can make your own Korean gimbap and enjoy a delicious taste of Korean culture. Noon, Troy Campus Library, “Chicken in a Strange Way: A SoCal Beach Girl’s Take on Communism.” Melanie Armstrong will discuss her book, “Chicken in a Strange Way,” that details the two years she spent in Prague, Czech Republic as it transitioned from communism to capitalism. Working for Arthur Anderson, Armstrong audited companies as they were being prepared to be sold from the state to the private sector. In the process, she learned how insane and frightening communism was. This event is free and is open to the public. This is a lunch and learn event, so feel free to bring a non-messy lunch. Free copies of “Chicken in a Strange Way” will be given away and Chick-Fil-A sandwiches will be given away while they last. 5:30 p.m., Lamar P. Higgins Ballrooms, second floor of the Trojan Center, ISCO Festival (tickets required). This content is sourced from Troy University Dothan Campus .
